text: The same field can grow peach trees or hold solar panels, and not both. Carla Simón builds a Catalan family's summer around that arithmetic: the Solés have picked this orchard every year, and someone has now worked out what the land is worth with the trees gone. The threat is a plan rather than a villain, which is the harder thing to put on a screen and the truer one. Most of the 118 minutes go to the picking - heat, crates, the small negotiations of a household whose days are organized so completely by the harvest that losing it means losing the shape of an afternoon. What eviction takes here is not shelter so much as the work that tells everyone in the house who they are and when to get up. It took the European Film Award for Best Film and for Best Screenwriter, with the European University Film Award beside them.

The war is over before this film starts, and that is the situation it takes on. Jasmila Žbanić works with two people, a woman and her daughter in postwar Bosnia, and with ninety minutes, which for this material is a discipline rather than a shortage. The mother's history is not narrated; it is carried, and it shows in the distance between what a household says out loud and what it quietly works around. Nothing is staged as testimony. The pressure sits under the daily business of getting by in a country where the fighting has stopped and very little else has been settled, and the two of them go on living inside it at close range. The film took the Golden Bear in 2006, and a European Film Award went to the performance at its centre, with another for the film itself.

Four stories, four men, and in each one a task the state needs an ordinary person to carry out. Mohammad Rasoulof sets his anthology against Iran's use of the death penalty, and the crisis he returns to is practical rather than legal: what happens to a man with a shift to finish and a family to get home to when he grasps what his own hands are being asked to do, and what refusing would cost him instead. The Golden Bear went to it in 2020. The production is registered in Germany and the dialogue is Persian, a combination that says something about the conditions under which the film reached a screen. Two and a half hours divided four ways gives each part its own tone; they are four films that happen to agree.

Two women live one floor apart, and neither is where she was meant to end up. Charlotte has walked out on a boyfriend and on a life she could have had and does not want; Veronica, a trans woman, stays in with a small dog and a television romance delivered in daily instalments. Pernille Fischer Christensen, who took a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize for this and a Bodil for Best Danish Film, keeps the whole thing inside one building and lets the comedy come from proximity: two people with nothing in common but a staircase, each having arranged her days so that nobody gets close enough to ask anything. The soap playing in the other flat is precisely the sort of feeling the film declines to manufacture for itself. What it offers instead is 105 minutes of two solitudes negotiating a single address.

Paris, 18 August 1572: a Catholic princess is married to a Protestant king so that a kingdom will not tear in half. Marguerite de Valois did not choose Henry III of Navarre and he did not choose her; her brother is the feeble Charles IX, and the crown he wears is not strong enough to hold whatever the wedding buys. Patrice Chéreau films a court where family business and state business are conducted in the same corridors, by the same people, at the same volume. The costume work took an Academy Award and a César, which in a story about a dynastic marriage is not decoration - what a person puts on is what they are announcing - and the César for Best Actress went to the film's centre. 138 minutes in French, and the peace it opens with is only as durable as a marriage nobody wanted.

A woman said a dingo took her baby from the tent, and a country spent years deciding whether to believe her. Fred Schepisi films the Chamberlain case from inside that argument rather than at Ayers Rock: what he follows is the machinery afterwards - the searching, two public inquests, a murder charge - and the far larger informal court made up of people who were not there and had views anyway. The AACTA awards went to the two leads and to the screenplay, which is the right distribution for a film assembled out of hearings, statements and secondhand certainty. Australian, 1989, 120 minutes. The weight falls on how a person is read by strangers, and on what happens to a mother whose grief does not perform itself the way strangers have decided grief should.

The maid gives notice: after a stroke, the woman who has kept somebody else's household says she would like to stop and move into a home for the old. Ann Hui treats that request as the whole of her plot. What follows is less a reversal than a slow correction - the family that employed her has to work out what it owes, in visits and fees and hours, to someone whose place among them was never given a name. The prizes came in a bunch: Best Film at the Hong Kong Film Awards, the Golden Horse for Best Feature, the Golden Rooster for Best Picture, a Volpi Cup for the performance at the centre. Hui is exact about the small economics of care and unhurried about everything else, and across 118 minutes almost nothing is raised above the level of an errand.

A hunter who can take an animal without spoiling the hide is worth more than the men around him, and they notice. Tizoc hands its central figure competence, wisdom and kindness, then makes each of those a reason he is resented, which turns the love story into a public matter rather than a private one: a man everyone is watching cannot court anyone quietly. What stands to be lost is standing itself - admiration and suspicion come from the same neighbours, in the same week, and a reputation is the one thing the film gives him to lose. Ismael Rodríguez shot it in Mexico in 1956, 109 minutes, and the honours landed where the film puts its weight: a Silver Bear for the leading performance, and the Ariel for Best Picture at home. Envy makes a modest engine for a drama. It needs no villain and no accident, only neighbours who can count.

Two hours and forty-four minutes, one town, and a stretch of history that kept revising who was permitted to speak to whom. Xie Jin adapted Gu Hua's novel in 1988, when much of the audience would have carried its own version of those years. The scale stays deliberately small: a young woman, a place where everyone is accounted for, neighbours whose positions relative to one another are rearranged by decisions taken somewhere else. It runs long because a change of that kind only registers against an ordinary life the film has taken its time to build. It collected the Crystal Globe, the Golden Rooster for Best Picture and the Huabiao. The melodrama is not a lapse of taste but the instrument: a political period is felt first as a change in who nods on the street, and only afterwards as anything with a name.

In 1884 a London heat wave empties the theatres and Gilbert and Sullivan's newest piece, Princess Ida, meets a lukewarm press. Mike Leigh gives 160 minutes to what happens next, and nearly all of it is work: two collaborators at odds over material, a borrowed Japanese setting being converted into an English hit, and the ordinary trade of getting a company onto a stage. The Academy Awards it won were for costume, makeup and production design - the departments the film is actually about, which is either coincidence or a very exact verdict. What Leigh withholds is the moment of inspiration. The Mikado arrives here as a product with a deadline, assembled by tired professionals, and the thing an audience would later call effortless is shown costing every hour it cost.

Three people attempt a friendship inside a country arranged to prevent it. An Indian doctor, an Englishwoman lately arrived and engaged to a city magistrate, and an English educator find one another congenial, which in British colonial India is not a private matter but a small breach of an order everybody else is busy maintaining. David Lean works at scale - 163 minutes, landscape, weather, an Academy Award for the cinematography - while the actual pressure is social, operating at the level of an invitation accepted or a remark left unanswered. Manners are the enforcement mechanism here. The Academy also gave the film Best Actress and Best Costume Design, and the New York critics and the National Board of Review both handed it their Best Film award; what it watches most closely is the distance between goodwill and everything goodwill cannot reach.

A cough is going around a Welsh mining town, and the new doctor is the only man treating it as a question rather than a fact of life. Andrew Manson is young, Scottish, newly qualified and entirely without leverage; when his attempt to establish where the cough comes from runs into people who would rather it stayed unestablished, he leaves for London, where the medicine that pays turns out to have little to do with the medicine he trained for. He is not tempted by wickedness, only by a comfortable living. King Vidor made this in Britain in 1938, at 110 minutes; the Academy noticed it in the largest categories - Picture, Director, Actor - and the New York critics gave it their Best Film award. The argument underneath is blunt: a profession can be practised honestly or profitably, and the pressure to choose arrives dressed as common sense.

A talent big enough to win with, attached to a temperament that will not let it. Fast Eddie Felson can beat nearly anyone with a cue and cannot leave a table while there is anything left to prove, so the match he chases - against Minnesota Fats, for stakes that hurt - is less a contest of skill than an examination of character. Robert Rossen shot it in black and white, and the Academy's attention went to the two leads and to the art direction: rooms, tables, and the light they are lit by. It is in the National Film Registry, and among the thousand films on the TSPDT list. 134 minutes, much of it people talking about winning while the balls stand still, because the subject here is stamina - how long a man can stay at a table, and what he turns into by refusing to leave it.

The family business is crime, and the person running it is somebody's grandmother. Joshua, known as J, moves in with his relatives after his mother's overdose, and the house he arrives at is calmer than it should be: the warmth in it is real, and it is also the mechanism by which he is brought in. David Michôd films the trade as a domestic arrangement, so the pressure sits at the kitchen table and in what a person is permitted to notice; when a policeman offers J another road, that offer is inseparable from informing on the people who took him in. Three AACTA acting awards followed, and Australian critics later placed the film in their top twenty-five of the century so far. 113 minutes, and the tension is almost entirely conversational.
